title: RELATIVE PRONOUNS & RELATIVE CLAUSES
notes:
✓ Relative pronoun → a word that introduces a relative clause and connects it to a noun or pronoun in the main clause.

✓ Relative clause → a dependent clause that gives additional information about a noun or pronoun.

✓ The student who won the prize is my friend.

✓ Antecedent → the noun that the relative clause refers to.
✓ student = antecedent.
✓ who won the prize = relative clause.

✓ Relative clauses help combine sentences and avoid unnecessary repetition.

title: MAIN RELATIVE WORDS
notes:
◆ WHO → people; usually subject.
✓ The woman who teaches us is kind.

◆ WHOM → people; object, especially formal English.
✓ The man whom I met was a doctor.

◆ WHOSE → possession; people and sometimes things/animals.
✓ The student whose phone was lost reported it.

◆ WHICH → things and animals.
✓ The book which I bought is interesting.

◆ THAT → people, animals, and things in defining relative clauses.
✓ The student that won the prize is my friend.

◆ WHERE → places.
✓ This is the school where I studied.

◆ WHEN → times/dates.
✓ I remember the day when we first met.

◆ WHY → reason.
✓ I know the reason why she left.

title: WHO
notes:
✓ Who refers to people and normally functions as the subject of the relative clause.

✓ The teacher who helped me was very kind.
✓ The students who studied hard passed the exam.

✓ Pattern → person + who + verb.

✓ The man who lives next door is a doctor.

⚠ When who is the subject, it cannot normally be removed.
❌ The man lives next door is a doctor.
✓ The man who lives next door is a doctor.

✓ Who can be used in both defining and non-defining relative clauses.

title: WHOM
notes:
✓ Whom refers to people and functions as the object of the relative clause.

✓ The woman whom I met was a doctor.

✓ Pattern → person + whom + subject + verb.

✓ The person whom we invited arrived early.

✓ Whom is more formal than who when used as an object.

✓ The person whom I called...
✓ The person who I called... → common in everyday English.
✓ The person I called... → pronoun omitted.

✓ Formal test → replace the relative word with him/her/them.
✓ I met him → whom.
✓ He met me → who.

title: WHO VS WHOM
notes:
◆ WHO → subject of the relative clause.
✓ The man who called me is my teacher.
→ He called me.

◆ WHOM → object of the relative clause.
✓ The man whom I called is my teacher.
→ I called him.

✓ Easy test →
He/She/They → WHO.
Him/Her/Them → WHOM.

⚠ In modern informal English, who is very commonly used instead of whom, but whom remains important in formal writing and examinations.

title: WHOSE
notes:
✓ Whose expresses possession or relationship.

✓ The student whose book was lost came to the office.
✓ I met a woman whose son is a doctor.

✓ Whose can refer to people and, in appropriate contexts, animals or things.

✓ A company whose products are popular...

✓ Pattern → noun + whose + possessed noun.

✓ The boy whose bicycle was stolen...

⚠ Whose is different from who's.

✓ whose → possession.
✓ who's → who is / who has.

❌ The student who's book was lost...
✓ The student whose book was lost...

title: WHICH
notes:
✓ Which normally refers to things and animals.

✓ The car which I bought is new.
✓ The dog which won the competition was very fast.

✓ Which can be the subject or object.

✓ The computer which crashed was old. → subject.
✓ The computer which I bought was expensive. → object.

✓ Which is used in both defining and non-defining relative clauses.

⚠ Which is normally preferred instead of that in non-defining clauses.

❌ My car, that is very old, needs repair.
✓ My car, which is very old, needs repair.

title: THAT
notes:
✓ That can refer to people, animals, and things in defining relative clauses.

✓ The student that won the prize is my friend.
✓ The book that I bought is excellent.
✓ The dog that barked belongs to my neighbor.

✓ That can function as subject or object.

✓ The person that called me is here. → subject.
✓ The person that I called is here. → object.

⚠ That is normally NOT used after a comma in a non-defining relative clause.

❌ My brother, that lives in London, is a doctor.
✓ My brother, who lives in London, is a doctor.

✓ That is especially common in defining clauses because it is concise and natural.

title: WHERE
notes:
✓ Where refers to a place and normally means 'in/at/on which.'

✓ This is the school where I studied.
= This is the school at which I studied.

✓ Addis Ababa is the city where I was born.

✓ Where introduces a relative clause connected to a place.

⚠ Do not use where if the relative word itself is the direct object.

✓ The house where I live is large.
✓ The house which I bought is large.

❌ The house where I bought is large.
→ If 'house' is the object of bought, use which/that or omit the pronoun.

title: WHEN
notes:
✓ When refers to a time, date, period, or occasion.

✓ I remember the day when we met.
✓ 2020 was the year when many things changed.

✓ When can often be replaced by 'in/on/at which.'

✓ The day when we met...
= The day on which we met...

⚠ When is often optional when the structure remains grammatical.

✓ The day when we met.
✓ The day we met.
✓ The day on which we met.

✓ All can be correct, but style and formality differ.

title: WHY
notes:
✓ Why refers to a reason and is usually used after the noun reason.

✓ I know the reason why she left.
✓ That is the reason why I called you.

✓ Why can often be replaced by 'for which.'

✓ The reason why he resigned...
✓ The reason for which he resigned...

✓ In many sentences, why can be omitted.

✓ I know the reason why she left.
✓ I know the reason she left.

✓ Why is most commonly associated with reason.

title: DEFINING RELATIVE CLAUSES
notes:
✓ Defining relative clause → gives essential information needed to identify the person or thing being discussed.

✓ The students who studied hard passed the exam.

✓ Without the relative clause → 'The students passed the exam' changes the intended meaning because we do not know which students.

✓ No commas are used.

✓ Possible relative words → who, whom, whose, which, that, where, when, why.

✓ Defining = essential information.

✓ The book that you gave me is useful.
✓ The teacher who teaches mathematics is absent.

title: NON-DEFINING RELATIVE CLAUSES
notes:
✓ Non-defining relative clause → gives extra information that is not necessary to identify the noun.

✓ My brother, who lives in London, is a doctor.

✓ 'My brother' already identifies the person; the relative clause simply adds information.

✓ Commas are required.

✓ Common relative words → who, whom, whose, which, where, when.

⚠ That is normally not used in non-defining clauses.

❌ My car, that is old, needs repair.
✓ My car, which is old, needs repair.

⚠ The relative pronoun normally cannot be omitted in a non-defining clause.

title: DEFINING VS NON-DEFINING
notes:
◆ Defining → essential information; no commas.
✓ The students who passed the exam received certificates.

◆ Non-defining → extra information; commas required.
✓ The students, who passed the exam, received certificates.

⚠ These sentences can have different meanings.

✓ The students who passed... → only those students who passed.
✓ The students, who passed... → all the students passed; the clause adds information.

✓ Punctuation can change meaning.

title: OMITTING THE RELATIVE PRONOUN
notes:
✓ The relative pronoun can often be omitted when it functions as the object of the relative clause.

✓ The book that I bought is expensive.
✓ The book which I bought is expensive.
✓ The book I bought is expensive.

✓ All three are possible.

⚠ The pronoun cannot normally be omitted when it is the subject.

❌ The man lives next door is a doctor.
✓ The man who lives next door is a doctor.

✓ Object test → after the relative pronoun, there is already a subject.
✓ the book which I bought → I = subject, which = object.

✓ Subject test → the relative pronoun is followed directly by a verb.
✓ the man who lives here → who = subject.

title: RELATIVE PRONOUN AS OBJECT
notes:
✓ When the relative pronoun is the object, three forms are often possible in defining clauses.

✓ The woman whom I met was friendly.
✓ The woman who I met was friendly.
✓ The woman that I met was friendly.
✓ The woman I met was friendly.

✓ Formal → whom.
✓ Neutral/common → who or that.
✓ Concise → omission.

⚠ Omission is not normally possible when a preposition directly precedes the relative pronoun in a formal structure.

✓ The person to whom I spoke...
❌ The person to I spoke...

title: PREPOSITIONS + RELATIVE PRONOUNS
notes:
✓ Formal English can place a preposition before the relative pronoun.

✓ The person to whom I spoke was helpful.
✓ The company for which he works is international.
✓ The house in which they live is large.

✓ Informal English commonly places the preposition at the end.

✓ The person who I spoke to was helpful.
✓ The company which he works for is international.
✓ The house which they live in is large.

⚠ That cannot normally follow a preposition directly.

❌ The company for that he works.
✓ The company for which he works.

title: FORMAL RELATIVE STRUCTURES
notes:
✓ Formal patterns →

◆ person + to whom
◆ thing + to which
◆ thing + in which
◆ thing + on which
◆ thing + for which
◆ person + with whom

✓ The professor to whom I spoke was helpful.
✓ The organization for which she works is large.
✓ The room in which we met was crowded.
✓ The colleague with whom I worked was experienced.

✓ These structures are common in formal writing, academic English, and examinations.

title: WHICH REFERRING TO A WHOLE CLAUSE
notes:
✓ Which can refer to an entire preceding clause, not just one noun.

✓ He missed the bus, which made him late.

✓ Which refers to the fact that he missed the bus.

✓ She passed the exam, which surprised everyone.

⚠ This use is normally non-defining and requires a comma.

❌ He missed the bus that made him late. → different meaning; that normally refers to a noun.

✓ Comma + which can comment on the whole preceding situation.

title: WHOEVER / WHATEVER / WHICHEVER
notes:
✓ Whoever → any person who / no matter who.
✓ Whoever finishes first will win.

✓ Whatever → anything that / no matter what.
✓ Take whatever you need.

✓ Whichever → any one of a limited set.
✓ Choose whichever book you prefer.

✓ These are often called compound relative words or -ever forms.

◆ whoever = person
◆ whatever = thing
◆ whichever = choice from alternatives

✓ They can introduce noun clauses or free relative clauses depending on their function.

title: FREE RELATIVE CLAUSES
notes:
✓ Free relative clause → a relative clause that functions as a noun phrase without a separate antecedent.

✓ What you said was true.

✓ 'What you said' = the thing that you said.

✓ Whoever arrives first can enter.
✓ I will take whatever you offer.
✓ Choose whichever you prefer.

⚠ What is different from which.

✓ What you need is here. → no antecedent.
✓ The book which you need is here. → 'book' is antecedent.

✓ What often means 'the thing(s) that.'

title: WHAT VS WHICH
notes:
✓ What → normally does not have an antecedent before it.
✓ What I need is a break.

✓ Which → normally refers back to an antecedent.
✓ The book which I need is on the table.

❌ The book what I need...
✓ The book which/that I need...

❌ I don't know the thing what he wants.
✓ I don't know what he wants.

✓ Rule → If there is already a noun being described, use who/which/that/etc.; if there is no antecedent and you mean 'the thing that,' use what.

title: AGREEMENT IN RELATIVE CLAUSES
notes:
✓ The verb inside the relative clause agrees with the antecedent.

✓ The student who studies hard succeeds.
✓ The students who study hard succeed.

⚠ Do not let a nearby noun confuse the subject.

✓ The students who study mathematics are successful.
→ students = subject, so use are.

✓ The student who studies mathematics is successful.
→ student = subject, so use is.

✓ Identify the antecedent before choosing the verb.

title: COLLECTIVE NOUNS + RELATIVE CLAUSES
notes:
✓ When the antecedent is a collective noun, verb agreement depends on whether the group is treated as one unit or as individuals, especially in varieties of English.

✓ The team that is winning is confident.

✓ The team who are training... → possible in British-style usage when members are emphasized.

✓ For school/exam English, follow the agreement convention expected by the context and variety being taught.

title: RELATIVE WORDS FOR ANIMALS
notes:
✓ Animals can be referred to with which, that, or who depending on context and whether the animal is treated as an individual/pet.

✓ The dog that won the race was fast.
✓ The dog which won the race was fast.
✓ The dog who saved the child became famous. → possible when the animal is treated personally.

✓ That and which are common for animals; who can be used when the animal is personified or treated as a named individual.

title: WHERE VS WHICH + PREPOSITION
notes:
✓ The house where I live is beautiful.

✓ The house in which I live is beautiful.

✓ The house which I live in is beautiful.

✓ These can express essentially the same location relationship.

⚠ But the structures must be grammatically complete.

❌ The house where I bought is expensive.
✓ The house which I bought is expensive.

✓ 'Where' already contains the location relationship; 'which' needs the appropriate preposition when required.

title: WHEN VS WHICH
notes:
✓ The day when we met was memorable.

✓ The day on which we met was memorable.

❌ The day which we met... in this meaning, because the relationship requires 'on which' or 'when'.

✓ The day which I remember was memorable.
→ Here 'day' is the object of remember.

✓ The choice depends on the grammatical role of the antecedent inside the relative clause.

title: WHY VS THAT / WHICH
notes:
✓ The reason why he left is unknown.

✓ The reason that he left is unknown. → possible.

✓ The reason he left is unknown. → possible; relative marker omitted.

✓ The reason for which he left is unknown. → formal.

✓ Several structures can express the same relationship, but their style differs.

title: REDUCED RELATIVE CLAUSES
notes:
✓ A relative clause can sometimes be shortened when the relative pronoun is the subject.

✓ The man who is standing there is my teacher.
✓ The man standing there is my teacher.

✓ The books that were written by the professor are useful.
✓ The books written by the professor are useful.

✓ Active reduction → relative pronoun + be + V-ing can often become V-ing.

✓ Passive reduction → relative pronoun + be + V3 can often become V3.

✓ Reduced relatives make writing more concise and are common in academic English.

title: COMMON RELATIVE PRONOUN ERRORS
notes:
❌ The man which called me is my teacher.
✓ The man who called me is my teacher.

❌ The book who I bought is interesting.
✓ The book which/that I bought is interesting.

❌ The student who's book was lost...
✓ The student whose book was lost...

❌ My brother, that lives in London, is a doctor.
✓ My brother, who lives in London, is a doctor.

❌ The person to that I spoke...
✓ The person to whom I spoke...

❌ The place where I visited was beautiful.
✓ The place which/that I visited was beautiful.

❌ The reason which he left...
✓ The reason why he left...

❌ The book what I bought...
✓ The book that/which I bought...

❌ The man who I met him was friendly.
✓ The man who I met was friendly.

⚠ Do not use an extra object pronoun after a relative pronoun when the relative pronoun already performs that object function.

title: RELATIVE CLAUSE DOUBLE-OBJECT ERROR
notes:
✓ A common error is using both the relative pronoun and another pronoun for the same grammatical role.

❌ The woman who I met her was kind.

✓ The woman who I met was kind.
✓ The woman whom I met was kind.

❌ The book which I bought it is expensive.

✓ The book which I bought is expensive.

✓ One grammatical role should normally have one corresponding element. The relative pronoun already represents the antecedent inside the relative clause.

title: RELATIVE PRONOUN MASTER TABLE
notes:
◆ WHO → people; subject/object in common usage.

◆ WHOM → people; object, especially formal.

◆ WHOSE → possession; people and some non-human antecedents.

◆ WHICH → things/animals; defining and non-defining.

◆ THAT → people/things/animals; mainly defining clauses.

◆ WHERE → place/location.

◆ WHEN → time/date/period.

◆ WHY → reason.

◆ WHAT → the thing(s) that; no separate antecedent.

◆ WHOEVER → any person who.

◆ WHATEVER → anything that.

◆ WHICHEVER → any one from a limited choice.

title: RELATIVE PRONOUN DECISION GUIDE
notes:
✓ Is the antecedent a person? → WHO / WHOM / WHOSE / THAT.

✓ Is it a thing or animal? → WHICH / THAT / WHOSE.

✓ Does it express possession? → WHOSE.

✓ Is it a place? → WHERE or which/that + appropriate preposition.

✓ Is it a time? → WHEN or which + appropriate preposition.

✓ Is it a reason? → WHY / that / omission / for which.

✓ Is there no antecedent and you mean 'the thing that'? → WHAT.

✓ Is the relative clause essential? → Defining; no commas.

✓ Is the information extra? → Non-defining; commas required.

✓ Is the relative pronoun the object? → It can often be omitted in defining clauses.

✓ Is it the subject? → Do not omit it.

title: EXAM STRATEGY: RELATIVE PRONOUNS
notes:
◆ 1. Identify the antecedent → person, thing, place, time, reason, or possession.

◆ 2. Identify the grammatical role → subject or object.

◆ 3. Decide whether the clause is defining or non-defining.

◆ 4. Check whether a comma is required.

◆ 5. Choose the appropriate relative word.

◆ 6. Check whether the relative pronoun can be omitted.

◆ 7. Look for prepositions → to whom, for which, in which, etc.

◆ 8. Check that no extra pronoun is used.

◆ 9. Check subject-verb agreement inside the relative clause.

◆ 10. Check whether the sentence requires a formal or informal structure.

✓ Golden rules →
WHO = people.
WHOM = object/formal people.
WHOSE = possession.
WHICH = things/animals.
THAT = defining clauses.
WHERE = place.
WHEN = time.
WHY = reason.
WHAT = 'the thing that' without an antecedent.
